messages.author: 85679393b8bc3d9b
messages.subject: Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Hi all,

I have a phylogeny and 3-D morphometric data. I want to calculate trait disparity (euclidean dist) between sister species PC scores. Is there a function in geomorph that will do this for me or is there another way I should go about doing this in R?

Thanks,
Nick

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Nick,

In the form of a script,

fit <- procD.pgls(coords ~ 1, phy = myTree, …)
dist(fit$pgls.residuals)

By fitting a model with only an intercept, the distance matrix among species residuals is the same as the distance matrix among species values, after accounting for phylogeny.  If you rather use PC scores than coordinates,

PCA <- prcomp(fit$pgls.residuals)
dist(PCA$x)

You should get comparable results, regardless.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Nick,

Sorry I was not clearer in my previous post.  The … as a function argument means, “plus other arguments”.  The one you are missing is a geomorph data frame.  First you received a warning letting you know that you did not have a data and that if an error occurred, this might be the reason.  Then you received an error.  So my best guess for the error is because you did not use a data frame.

In terms of why you need one, that is a question that is not easy to answer.  A few years ago, CRAN made some updates that caused their model.frame/model.matrix functions to not behave well without a data frame.  We ask for a data frame so that we can give the underlying model functions a data frame.  When it does not work, we can only offer an explanation of ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ .  But we can tell you that if you use a geomorph data frame, the problem is generally resolved.  The procD.lm and procD.pgls examples all use geomorph data frames, so how to do this can be inferred through those examples.

Best,
Mike

messages.author: 85679393b8bc3d9b
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Hi Mike,

Is there a way to tell R/geomorph to restrict the disparity calculations to sister species only as opposed to calculating pairwise distances?

Nick

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Hi Nick,

Short answer, no.  The morphol.disparity function randomizes residuals from the model you define and calculates variances for the group you define.  There is no way to restrict which residuals it uses.  You could save the residuals and design your own test performed only on pairs if you like, but if that is the case, I’m not sure why one would use a more complex multi-species model in the first place.

Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Nick,

The morphol.disparity function details describe exactly what the function does, which is to randomize residuals among groups, many times, calculate Procrustes variance for each group, and compare these in pairwise fashion.  If a pairwise procedure is not what you desire or think is relevant, the beautiful thing about R is that you can take the code for the function and modify it for your specific needs.  The function is not designed to perform planned contrasts like one might do in parametric ANOVA.  If you seek something like that, you might consider writing your own function for it.

Mike
On Nov 4, 2018, at 6:46 PM, Nick <nvin...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Mike,

Is there any reason one would not one to calculate disparity among all pairwise comparisons via random permutation of the 10 species when I just want the sister species contrasts? Like, is there a better way to go about this?

Nick

On Sunday, November 4, 2018 at 2:01:52 PM UTC-8, Michael Collyer wrote:
Nick,

You are free to pick out the five differences that are important to you and disregard the rest.  But if there are 10 species in the test then the residuals have to be randomly permuted across 10 species.  The alternative is to perform the test 5 times on species pairs, which I would not recommend as better.

Mike

On Nov 4, 2018, at 4:57 PM, Nick <nvin...@gmail.com> wrote:

Many thanks for your reply Mike. So I have a tree pruned only to sister species and then calculated disparity among them using the function above but the resulting pairwise distance matrix is more than I need. For example, if I had 10 species that would result in 100 pairwise comparisons, where all I want is the 5 sister species contrasts.

On Sunday, November 4, 2018 at 1:28:36 PM UTC-8, Michael Collyer wrote:
Hi Nick,

Short answer, no.  The morphol.disparity function randomizes residuals from the model you define and calculates variances for the group you define.  There is no way to restrict which residuals it uses.  You could save the residuals and design your own test performed only on pairs if you like, but if that is the case, I’m not sure why one would use a more complex multi-species model in the first place.

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Hi Mike,

The first 4 PC axes explain 95% of the variation in my data. Would calculating euclidean distance from PCA as you suggest,

PCA <- prcomp(fit$pgls.residuals)
dist(PCA$x),

run the risk of underestimating (deflating) estimates of disparity? I can imagine restricting the trait disparity analysis to the first 4 axes would give a different answer as opposed to using all of them.

Thanks,

Nick
On Sunday, September 16, 2018 at 5:06:19 PM UTC-7, Michael Collyer wrote:

Nick,

In the form of a script,

fit <- procD.pgls(coords ~ 1, phy = myTree, …)
dist(fit$pgls.residuals)

By fitting a model with only an intercept, the distance matrix among species residuals is the same as the distance matrix among species values, after accounting for phylogeny.  If you rather use PC scores than coordinates,

PCA <- prcomp(fit$pgls.residuals)
dist(PCA$x)

You should get comparable results, regardless.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Nick,

Anytime you use only a subspace projection - to project data onto a subset of eigenvectors instead of the full rank of eigenvectors - you distort the relationship among observations to some degree.  How critical this distortion is will depend on the relative span of eigenvectors (how much variation is explained) and the dispersion of observations (outliers might really cause distortion).

Why somebody would want to do this is probably a more interesting question to entertain.

Mike

parts:
Dear all,

My question might not be directly in line with Nick's question, but it's about the the same function, morphol.disparity. Basically, I want to calculate the disparity for a set of species, controlling for allometry. I'm using the following command:

A)
morphol.disparity(f1 = shape ~ log(size)+species, groups= ~species iter = 9999, data = data, print.progress = TRUE)

This gives different disparity per group when compared to this:
B)
morphol.disparity(shape~log(size),groups=~species,iter=9999,data=data,print.progress = TRUE)

From what I understand from the function examples, in A we use the overall mean while on B we use the group means to calculate Procrustes variance. From a biological point of view I don't understand exactly the difference the between the questions answered by A and B. My question is, accounting for allometry, and considering a model with different species, which one displays the largest Procrustes variance. I guess in this case I should be looking at the results of A. My question now is what would B answer to and why are the disparity measurements contrasting.

Thanks in advance for your attention.

Best,
Sérgio.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
parts:
Sérgio,

The answer to your second question is simpler: shape ~ log(size) + species has different residuals than shape ~ log(size).  The groups = ~species part explains simply how to aggregate residuals.  Because the residuals are different the variances will be different.

A reason a person might choose to do B is to ascertain if one group happens to diverge more than others from a mean form, accounting for allometry, not in terms of a group mean but in terms of the individual observations.  This might not seem logical - and that might be perfectly appropriate to conclude for your data - but the flexibility of using residuals from any source model allows researchers to develop their own analyses without imposed dogma about how the data must be analyzed.  

Hope that helps
Mike
